lead: A blockchain that is secure and spread across many nodes is slow. A fast one usually asks you to trust fewer parties. Throughput, latency, storage, privacy and decentralisation pull against each other, and every design picks a point on that trade-off. This chapter measures the limits — transactions per second, bytes added per day — and surveys the standard fixes: bigger blocks, sharding, rollups, payment channels, private data and zero-knowledge proofs. It then covers regulation, energy, interoperability and quantum risk.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for channels and peers, plus consensus from Unit 3 and the limitations listed in Unit 4.

blocks.text: The scalability trilemma says a chain can hold only two of three at once: decentralisation (many independent validators), security (high cost to attack), and scalability (high transactions per second at low fees). It is a design trade-off, not a law of physics, but it explains why a public chain running on thousands of ordinary machines cannot match a payment network's throughput.

blocks.where: TPS is committed transactions per second; T is the number of transactions in one block; Δt is the block interval in seconds.

blocks.text: Storage is the second limit. Every full node keeps every block forever, so the ledger grows by T × s bytes every Δt seconds, where s is the average bytes per transaction record. High TPS without pruning or checkpointing pushes ordinary nodes off the network, which quietly cuts decentralisation.

items: Bigger blocks raise T but take longer to propagate, so forks and stale blocks become more likely (see Unit 3, forks).
A shorter Δt raises TPS the same way, at the same risk.
Throughput is not latency: finality time can stay slow even when TPS is high.

blocks.text: A layer-1 change edits the base protocol. Sharding splits the state and the validator set into k shards, each processing its own transactions, for roughly k times the throughput; cross-shard transactions then need extra messaging rounds and lose cheap atomicity.

A layer-2 change moves work off the chain but keeps its security. A rollup runs transactions off-chain and posts compressed data plus a proof back: an optimistic rollup assumes correctness and allows a challenge window, a ZK rollup posts a validity proof. A payment channel locks funds once on-chain, swaps many signed updates off-chain, and settles once. Side chains run their own consensus, so they are cheaper but borrow little security from layer 1.

Permissioned platforms get privacy from topology instead. In Fabric a channel limits who sees a transaction, and a private data collection puts a hash on-chain and the payload in a side database that only endorsed parties can read through chaincode.

sections.h3: Privacy, law, energy and long-term risk

items: Zero-knowledge proofs show a statement is true — 'this transfer is valid' — without revealing amounts, addresses or the witness. zk-SNARKs are small but usually need a trusted setup; zk-STARKs avoid it using hashes alone, with larger proofs.

KYC and AML rules push licensed businesses towards identified, permissioned ledgers. Data-protection law gives people a right to correction or erasure, which an append-only ledger cannot honour, so personal data stays off-chain and only a hash goes on.
Proof of Work pays for security in electricity; Proof of Stake pays in bonded capital and uses far less energy per transaction (see Unit 3, Proof of Stake).
Bridges lock an asset on one chain and mint a wrapped copy on another; the bridge, not either chain, holds the funds, which is why bridge failures have been the largest single loss point in practice.
Shor's algorithm would break ECDSA signatures on a large quantum computer. Hash-linked data survives better, and post-quantum signature schemes are the migration path.

spec.aria: Boxes: one block of 1,000 transactions and 500,000 bytes, divided by 12 seconds gives 83.33 per second; 7,200 blocks a day times 500,000 bytes gives 3.6 GB a day; a note on the cost to full nodes.

examples.question: A chain makes blocks every 12 s. Each block holds 1,000 transactions, and each transaction record is 500 bytes. Find the throughput in tx/s, the number of blocks per day, and the ledger growth per day in GB (use 1 GB = 10⁹ bytes).
steps: Read the data: block interval Δt = 12 s, transactions per block T = 1,000, average record size s = 500 bytes, seconds per day = 86,400.
Bytes per day = blocks per day × T × s = 7,200 × 1,000 × 500 = 3,600,000,000 bytes.
examples.answer: Throughput is 83.33 tx/s, the chain adds 7,200 blocks per day, and the ledger grows by 3.6 GB per day.
examples.check:
tx_per_block = 1000
block_seconds = 12
record_bytes = 500
tps = tx_per_block / block_seconds
blocks_per_day = 86400 / block_seconds
daily_bytes = blocks_per_day * tx_per_block * record_bytes
print(round(tps, 2))
print(int(blocks_per_day))
print(int(daily_bytes))
print(round(daily_bytes / 1e9, 2))

traps: Quoting TPS without Δt: 1,000 transactions per block means nothing until you divide by the block interval.
Confusing throughput with latency: a chain can commit many transactions per second and still take minutes to reach finality.
Unit slip: 3.6 × 10⁹ bytes is 3.6 GB, not 3.6 MB and not 36 GB. Keep the 10⁹ divisor explicit.
Treating rollups and side chains as the same thing: a rollup posts proofs or data to layer 1, a side chain runs its own consensus.
Assuming zero-knowledge means anonymous: the proof hides the witness, but the transaction, its timing and its fee are still visible.

quiz.a: A chain can strongly hold only two of decentralisation, security and scalability at a time; the third is weakened.

quiz.q: Define TPS and write its formula.
quiz.a: TPS is committed transactions per second: TPS = T ÷ Δt, with T transactions per block and block interval Δt seconds.

quiz.q: Why does doubling the block size not double real scalability for free?
quiz.a: It raises T but doubles propagation and storage per block, so stale blocks and fork rate rise and full nodes need more disk, bandwidth and time to sync — decentralisation falls.

quiz.q: A chain makes blocks every 10 s, each holding 500 transactions of 400 bytes. Find TPS and daily ledger growth in GB.
Sharding gives roughly k times the throughput. Why does it make cross-shard transfers harder?
quiz.a: Each shard validates only its own state, so a transfer touching two shards needs locking, messaging and receipts across shards; atomicity and safety need extra protocol rounds, and a shard can stall the whole transfer.

quiz.q: How does a Fabric channel differ from a private data collection as a privacy tool?
quiz.a: A channel is a separate ledger visible only to its members; a private data collection keeps the payload off-ledger and shares only its hash with channel members, revealing it to the subset named in the policy.

quiz.q: Why have cross-chain bridges been a repeated point of large losses?
quiz.a: The bridge contract or validator set custodies locked funds on one chain while minting a representation on the other, so it becomes a single high-value target; a bug or a key compromise drains the pool without breaking either chain.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems now mix layers: rollups on Ethereum, Fabric channels inside banks, and anchored hashes between them. Data-availability sampling, danksharding and validity proofs are the active research areas, and post-quantum signature schemes are moving from papers into test networks. Search for 'data availability sampling', 'zkEVM', and 'post-quantum blockchain signatures' to go deeper. Read blockchain bridge incident reports for concrete failure patterns.
